narrative:
The model determined that you have a 75.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is quite high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your class rank at the end of your third year was the strongest influence; being in the second decile is well below the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among accepted students, and this substantially pushed the prediction toward failure. Your first-year class rank came next; placing in the third decile instead of the typical sixth-decile level among accepted applicants further increased the estimated risk of not passing the bar. Your LSAT score, while still important, worked in the opposite direction. At 29.3 it is noticeably lower than the 37.2 average of accepted students, yet the model interpreted this particular score as providing a modest pull toward eventual success rather than failure.

Taken together, the below-average academic standing in law school itself outweighed the other signals and led the system to conclude your likelihood of passing the bar was too low to justify admission.

What you should do next is focus on raising your class rank as quickly as possible and retaking the LSAT to bring that score closer to the mid-30s or higher. Strong improvement in either area could meaningfully change future predictions and open the door to admission.
